Prior distributions for the coefficients of a penalized fit

Source: R/prior.R
coef_prior.Rd

Specifies independent priors centred at zero for the coefficients of mnl() and rologit() (prior = coef_prior(...)): the fit maximizes the log-likelihood plus the log prior density, the posterior mode. Under separation the maximum-likelihood estimates do not exist, and the prior (like Firth's penalty, firth = TRUE, which is Jeffreys' prior) decides how large the separated estimates are (Rainey 2016). Jeffreys' prior is a default justified by bias reduction; it depends on the design and is not independent across coefficients, and can move an estimate against the direction of the separation (Beiser-McGrath 2022). Independent priors make the assumption explicit, and fitting under several (a skeptical, an informative and an enthusiastic scale, Firth's penalty, and Gelman et al.'s default) shows how much of a separated estimate comes from the prior.

Usage

coef_prior(
  family = c("cauchy", "normal", "t"),
  scale = 2.5,
  df = NULL,
  intercept_scale = 10,
  autoscale = TRUE
)

Arguments

family

"cauchy" (default), "normal", or "t" (Student t with df degrees of freedom).

scale

The prior scale of the slopes (default 2.5). A named vector sets the scale of the coefficients it names (by their names in coef()), and an unnamed element, if any, the default for the others: a separated coefficient can be given a prior of its own (Rainey's partial prior). With autoscale, a named scale is divided by its column's scale like the default. A name the model does not have is ignored with a message, so the restricted model of a penalized likelihood-ratio test (lr_test()) can take the full model's prior.

df

Degrees of freedom of the t prior (family = "t" only).

intercept_scale

The prior scale of the constants (default 10).

autoscale

If TRUE (default), the slopes' scales are relative to their columns (see Details); if FALSE, they are on the coefficients as they are. The column scales use the frequency weights, so a fit whose weights total at most 2 (normalized or survey weights, which are not frequency weights) is refused under autoscale = TRUE: rescale the weights to counts, or set autoscale = FALSE. A scale named for a coefficient the model lacks is ignored with a message, which suggests a near match when the name looks like a misspelling.

Value

An object of class "coef_prior".

Details

The defaults are Gelman et al.'s (2008): Cauchy priors with scale 2.5 for the slopes and 10 for the constants, on coefficients scaled to the input. With autoscale = TRUE the scale of coefficient \(k\) is divided by \(c_k\): twice the standard deviation of its column when the column takes more than two values, the difference of its two values when it takes two (a dummy), as arm::bayesglm does. The column scales are taken over the estimation cases for a case-specific covariate and over the available alternatives for an alternative-specific (generic) one (the spread across all available alternatives, between cases as well as within them; Gelman et al.'s inputs are case-level, and the conditional logit's within-case spread would be the closer analogue), with the frequency weights (a weighted fit and the fit to the rows repeated by their weights get the same prior). The constants (the intercept of the case-specific part, which gives the alternative-specific constants) take intercept_scale, unscaled. The covariates are not centred, unlike Gelman et al.'s inputs, so the constants' prior concerns the log odds where every covariate is zero: centre a covariate whose zero lies far from its values (a calendar year) for that prior to mean what it says. With scale 2.5 a normal prior puts 95 percent of its mass on log odds within about 5 per two standard deviations of a covariate; the default Cauchy, with its heavier tails, puts 30 percent beyond 5. The prior's normalizing constants are left out of the penalized log-likelihood (they do not depend on the coefficients).

The fit reports the log-likelihood at the posterior mode (loglik), the maximized objective (loglik_penalized), and the inverse of the curvature of the log posterior at the mode as the covariance (the model's information plus the prior's curvature). arm::bayesglm differs for t and Cauchy priors: its approximate EM algorithm reports a related, always positive definite matrix at its own fixed point, and the two agree for the normal prior. For a t or Cauchy prior far out in its tail the exact curvature can fail to be positive definite (a separated coefficient); the prior's negative curvature is then left out, with a warning. Profile penalized-likelihood intervals (confint()) and penalized likelihood-ratio tests (term_test(), combine_test(), lr_test() between fits with the same prior, rank_test()) are the recommended inference under separation, as for Firth's penalty.

References

Beiser-McGrath, L.F. (2022). Separation and rare events. Political Science Research and Methods, 10, 428-437. doi:10.1017/psrm.2020.46

Gelman, A., Jakulin, A., Pittau, M.G. and Su, Y.-S. (2008). A weakly informative default prior distribution for logistic and other regression models. Annals of Applied Statistics, 2, 1360-1383. doi:10.1214/08-AOAS191

Rainey, C. (2016). Dealing with separation in logistic regression models. Political Analysis, 24, 339-355. doi:10.1093/pan/mpw014

See also

mnl(), rologit(), separation()

Examples

data(defection)
## the birth year centred, so that the constants' prior concerns typical respondents
defection$birth_c <- defection$birth_year - round(mean(defection$birth_year, na.rm = TRUE))
f <- outcome ~ economic * indoctrination + age_joined + birth_c + school_age + male
mc <- mnl(f, data = defection, ref = "captured", prior = coef_prior())
#> The maximum-likelihood estimates of demobilized:economic, demobilized:economic:indoctrination, switched:economic, switched:economic:indoctrination diverge (separation); their penalized estimates are determined largely by the penalty. Profile penalized-likelihood intervals (confint()) and penalized likelihood-ratio tests are the recommended inference.
mn <- mnl(f, data = defection, ref = "captured", prior = coef_prior("normal", scale = 4.5))
#> The maximum-likelihood estimates of demobilized:economic, demobilized:economic:indoctrination, switched:economic, switched:economic:indoctrination diverge (separation); their penalized estimates are determined largely by the penalty. Profile penalized-likelihood intervals (confint()) and penalized likelihood-ratio tests are the recommended inference.
cbind(cauchy = coef(mc), normal = coef(mn))
#>                                          cauchy       normal
#> demobilized:(Intercept)              0.17715211  0.100825330

#> demobilized:indoctrination           0.05477713  0.035840505
